name: Vivid black
lede: Vivid black is a near-black, violet-tinged neutral that our data pairs with the Japanese traditional name 黒紅 (Kurobeni), literally "dark red," and it is one of the more common colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A name that reads darker than it translates
sections.body:
Our source files this hue under the Japanese traditional color list as 黒紅 (Kurobeni), whose literal meaning in our data is "dark red" even though the swatch itself reads as a near-black neutral with a faint violet cast [1]. That gap is a translation and categorization quirk carried in our traditional-color sources, not a documented dye difference [1]. The English label "Vivid black" is our library's plain descriptive name for the same hex [1].

Its nearest look-alikes are [[pale-black-shade]] and [[pale-black-shade]] (both 2.9 units, almost the same), [[raisin-black]] (5.0, almost the same) and [[continental-blue]] (5.5, lighter) [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 1,134 of 23,781 paintings, about 4.77 percent, as photographed, more common than 90 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1500s, found in 5.7 percent of the 2,231 paintings we have from then (127 paintings), 1.2 times the expected rate for that century, and plays a shadow tone in 51 percent of the paintings that carry it [3]. George Dawe is its most devoted painter, using it in 18 of his 50 works here, 3.7 times the baseline rate for the museums those works come from [3]. It is most over-represented in paintings from the United Kingdom, at 2.3 times the expected rate, and shares canvases more than chance with Wine Brown and Marigold [3]. The earliest dated match is 1201, a floor set by thin early-century coverage rather than a true first [3].
